title: Idwal's Brilliant Blunder
markdown:
Mariner's Cove usually kept its salt air as steady as a well-tuned box. Today Idwal Buttercup, park keeper, had a moth of a flutter under his vest. He was a marmalade cat, peach-furred, whiskers on duty for every small sound. The forest-green waistcoat felt tight. The Seagull Serenade picnic began in one hour, the year's big gathering, and Idwal, who had been sincerely studying dandelions, had lost the instructions. Not a shopping list. The instructions: driftwood seats, seashell grammar, the secret in the seed cakes.

"Oh, crumbs."

"Right then, Jun." A little too loud. Jun the rat, bead-black eyes, mind like a busy clock, was polishing a brass bell. "The arrangements will be very creative today."

Jun's whiskers ticked. "Creative, Idwal? Or mixed up. Unplanned."

Idwal's tail flicked, the private flag. "Exactly. Happy surprise. Why follow old rules when we can have an adventure?" He went, generous of shape and suddenly quick, humming more thrill than tune. Jun sighed a small name after him. Idwal was already draping picnic blankets over lampposts. Extra height. A touch of fun. The knot had more energy than skill.

Mrs. Higgins arrived next, neighbour, honey-cake authority, floral dress a cheerful sail. "The special umbrella for shade. Isn't it wonderful?"

She opened it. Sequins. Peacock feathers. A disco of shade, almost too bright to be useful. This had not been in the forgotten paper.

"Mrs. Higgins. So grand. So beautiful. Extra sparkle. Flair." His fur prickled. The umbrella threw green coins of light across the grass and looked very sure of itself.

Townsfolk came, curious. Old Captain Flint, bagpipes already wheezy, peered at the lamppost linen. "Catching high-flying notes, are you?" He tuned with a noise like a startled goose. Miss Petunia the librarian, glasses at the end of a long patience, studied the seashells Idwal had set in twisty, silly maps. "I don't remember this star in Myths of the Sea."

"Modern design," Idwal said, smile on a lean. "Very new."

Then the gulls, who treat a picnic as a committee meeting with wings. He had meant to keep them busy with stale crusts on a far patch, his decoys, a diplomatic offering. The real seed cakes sat on the main tables, smelling like the truth and a little of honey. Gulls, who can read a menu, chose the truth. They arrived as white weather, loud opinions, a whirlwind that made the lawn look briefly snowed. Cakes vanished. Crumbs took office in every direction. Sequins on the umbrella shivered as if joining the board. Blankets, wind-caught, rustled like bad decisions trying to fly. Flint's pipes found a wobbly distance and stayed there, arguing with a squawk and nearly winning.

Idwal sat into a deckchair. Tail a sad flower. The creative day had become a feathered argument. Jun ran his leg and took the shoulder, claws a small comfort.

"Not quite the Serenade," Jun said.

Idwal shook his head. A rumble in the chest. "I forgot. Everything. A mess."

Jun nudged an ear. "Sometimes the good traditions are the ones we invent. And I remembered a few things." From a hidden pocket, a flourish: the original parchment, tiny, rolled, intact.

Idwal's smile arrived slow. Confused faces. Gulls still looping. The dazzling shade. He stood. Tail firm.

"This is not the Seagull Serenade picnic." Clear, through the squawk. "This is the Mariner's Cove Accidental Aerial Art Festival and Picnic Promenade."

He told them Jun had found the paper. He did not call it a rescue so much as a start nobody had had the nerve to schedule. Blankets came down from the lampposts, grass-stained and grand, and went up again as forts with doors of opinion. Children approved and immediately invented ranks. Gulls, recast as a troupe, received more crumbs and flew the show in loops that would never pass an exam; the giggling was official and loud enough to count as programme notes. Mrs. Higgins' umbrella was named Festival Centrepiece and looked relieved to have a title, peacock feathers nodding like a modest crowd. Flint found a beat in the noise and played something lively and only slightly wild, a serenade that had taken a wrong turning and liked the view.

Idwal's vest still felt tight. He did not mind. Jun's parchment stayed in the rat's pocket, a fact, not a scolding. On the lawn the forts listed, the cakes were a memory of crumbs, and the peacock shade threw green coins for anyone who wanted them. Idwal Buttercup, who had studied the dandelions at the wrong moment, watched a gull bow by accident and decided the picnic had, in its own weather, begun.
characters: Idwal (earnest cat park keeper), Jun (rat friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
